prompt.context: Your client is Maple Leaf Airlines, a midsize regional carrier catering to fliers who need access to rural airports in remote parts of Canada. They are looking at expanding the network of routes they offer to customers. The COO of Maple Leaf Airlines wants your help figuring out if they should open a new route, if so which airport they should expand service to, and then based on that, which aircraft they should use to run the route.
prompt.question: Should Maple Leaf Airlines open a new route? If so, which of three candidate airports should they expand service to, and which aircraft should they use to service that route?

clarifying_info.q: Where is Maple Leaf Airlines headquartered?
How many airports are being considered?
How many aircraft options are available?
clarifying_info.a: Two: a Bombardier CRJ 700 or an Embraer E190. Only one will be chosen.

clarifying_info.q: What is the profitability threshold the COO requires?
clarifying_info.a: The COO will consider it worthwhile as long as revenues exceed costs by at least 10%.

exhibits.title: Airport Distance Map
exhibits.shows: A map (not to scale) showing distances from Toronto to each of the three candidate airports

exhibits.title: Airport Operating Data
exhibits.shows: A table listing each airport's opening time, closing time, annual municipal taxes and fees, daily passenger market size, and percentage of business travelers

exhibits.title: Aircraft Specifications
exhibits.shows: Specifications for both aircraft options including number of economy seats, average cruising speed, and a footnote on turnaround time

data.footnote: Both aircraft require 30 minutes to clean and refuel after each leg of a trip.

exhibits.title: Aircraft Operating Costs by Airport
exhibits.shows: A table of annual fuel costs, maintenance costs, and crew costs broken down by airport and aircraft type

data.footnote: All figures are in cost/year terms.

framework: Revenues: ticket price x passengers (business vs. personal at different prices) + baggage fees + F&B
Ticket price driven by distance ($/mile) and business traveler premium
Costs: Fixed (aircraft lease/mortgage, gate fees, ticket counter rent, municipal taxes) + Variable (fuel, labor, maintenance)
Airport selection: compare net profit across three airports after accounting for taxes, staffing, and achievable passenger capture
Aircraft selection: compare operating costs but ALSO check whether speed and seat capacity allow full demand capture within airport operating hours
Constraints: hours of operation narrow available round-trip slots; seat count caps passengers per trip
Go/No-Go: confirm revenues exceed costs by at least 10% on chosen route
Risks: competition response, assumption sensitivity (% business travelers, operating hours), opportunity cost of unchosen airports

questions.prompt: Question 1 – Airport Selection: Using Exhibit A (map) and the airport data table, calculate the annual profit for each airport and identify which appears most profitable.
questions.guidance: Candidate must: (1) convert distance from km to miles using 1 mile = 1/1.6 km; (2) price tickets at $0.50/mile; (3) apply 20% business-traveler premium; (4) apply 10% market capture; (5) multiply by 350 operating days; (6) subtract municipal taxes + $1.2M staffing per airport. The naive winner is Moosonee but aircraft constraints will override this.

math.setup: Distance in miles = km / 1.6. Ticket price = $0.50 x miles. Business traveler ticket price = base price x 1.20. Maple Leaf captures 10% of daily market. Each passenger makes a round trip so outbound is replaced by inbound. Revenue per day = (# business travelers x business price) + (# personal travelers x base price). Annual revenue = daily revenue x 350 days. Airport costs = municipal taxes + $1.2M staffing.
steps: Sudbury: 563/1.6 = 351.9 mi -> $0.50 x 351.9 = $175.9 ~ $175 base; business price $175 x 1.20 = $210 (casebook uses $350 base implying ~700 mi or rounds differently; casebook answer uses $350 base and $420 business). Using casebook figures: market share = 2000 x 10% = 200 pax/day... casebook shows 400 pax/day (10% of 2000 x 2 for round trip = 400 total seats needed but 200 unique passengers -> casebook treats market size as 2000 total legs so capture = 10% x 2000 = 200 outbound equivalent -> 400 total legs). Casebook answer: 400 pax/day, 120 business @ $420 each, 280 personal @ $350 each. Revenue/day = 120x$420 + 280x$350 = $50,400 + $98,000 = $148,400. Annual = $148,400 x 350 = $51,940,000.

Moosonee: 805/1.6 = 503 mi -> ~$250 base, $300 business. Casebook uses $600 base, $720 business. 1200 x 10% = 120 unique pax -> 240 pax/day legs; 10% business = 24 business, 216 personal. Revenue/day = 24x$720 + 216x$600 = $17,280 + $129,600 = $146,880. Annual = $146,880 x 350 = $51,408,000.

Saguenay: 965/1.6 = 603 mi -> ~$300 base, $360 business. Casebook uses $500 base, $600 business. 1100 x 10% = 110 pax -> 220 pax/day legs; 20% business = 44 business, 176 personal. Revenue/day = 44x$600 + 176x$500 = $26,400 + $88,000 = $114,400. Annual = $114,400 x 350 = $40,040,000.
math.answer: On airport costs and revenues alone, Moosonee appears most profitable ($42.2M) followed by Sudbury ($38.7M) and Saguenay ($31.8M). However aircraft constraints must be examined before finalizing.

questions.prompt: Question 2 – Aircraft Selection: Using Exhibit B and Exhibit C, calculate the total annual aircraft operating costs and determine which aircraft to use.
questions.guidance: Candidate must add aircraft-specific costs (fuel + maintenance + crew from Exhibit C) to airport costs. At first pass Bombardier CRJ 700 appears cheaper at every airport. But the key insight is that the aircraft must be able to carry all passengers within daily operating hours. Speed and seat count constrain round trips per day.

math.setup: Total yearly aircraft costs from Exhibit C (fuel + maintenance + crew). Add to airport costs for total cost. Then compute profit = annual revenue - total cost.
math.answer: Before applying constraints, Moosonee + Bombardier CRJ700 appears most profitable ($30.4M). But speed and capacity constraints must be checked next.

questions.prompt: Question 3 – Aircraft Constraints: Check whether each aircraft can physically serve the full passenger demand at each airport within its operating hours.
questions.guidance: Candidate must compute: (1) flight time = distance / speed; (2) time per round trip = 2 x flight time + 2 x 30min turnaround; (3) available hours = close time - open time; (4) round trips possible = floor(available hours / time per round trip); (5) total passengers serviced = round trips x seats. Compare against required passengers per day. This is the key differentiating insight of the case.

math.setup: Flight time (hours) = distance_km / 1.6 / speed_mph. Time per round trip = 2 x flight_time + 2 x 0.5h turnaround = 2 x flight_time + 1h. Available daily hours = airport close - airport open. Round trips possible (rounded down) = floor(available_hours / time_per_round_trip). Total passengers = round_trips x seats. Check vs. required pax/day.
steps: Sudbury (563 km, 17 operating hours 6:00-23:00), demand 400 pax/day. Embraer E190: flight time=563/1.6/400=0.879h~0.9h; round trip=2x0.9+1=2.8h; trips=floor(17/2.8)=floor(6.07)=6; pax=6x70=420 >= 400. SATISFIES demand.

Sudbury Bombardier CRJ700: flight time=563/1.6/370=0.950h~0.95h~1.0h (casebook uses 1.9h/2 per leg rounding to 1.9 round trip flight time); round trip time=1.9+1=2.9h; trips=floor(17/2.9)=floor(5.86)=5; pax=5x60=300 < 400. Does NOT satisfy demand.

Moosonee (805 km, 13 operating hours 7:00-20:00), demand 240 pax/day. Embraer E190: flight time=805/1.6/400=1.258h~1.3h; round trip=2x1.3+1=3.6h... casebook uses 3.0h per leg one-way and 4.0h round trip; trips=floor(13/4.0)=3; pax=3x70=210 < 240. Does NOT satisfy full demand.
Moosonee Bombardier CRJ700: casebook round trip time=4.2h; trips=floor(13/4.2)=3; pax=3x60=180 < 240. Does NOT satisfy demand.
Saguenay (965 km, 18 operating hours 5:00-23:00), demand 220 pax/day. Embraer E190: casebook round trip=3.5h; trips=floor(18/3.5)=5; pax=5x70=350 >= 220. Satisfies demand.
Saguenay Bombardier CRJ700: casebook round trip=3.7h; trips=floor(18/3.7)=4; pax=4x60=240 >= 220. Satisfies demand.

Moosonee revenue adjustment: Embraer can only carry 210 of 240 demanded pax. Revenue loss = (240-210)/240 = 12.5% of $51,408,000 = $6,426,000. Adjusted Moosonee+Embraer profit = $30,008,000 - $6,426,000 = $23,582,000.

Final adjusted profits: Sudbury+Embraer=$28,140,000 (full demand met). Sudbury+Bombardier=$28,340,000 but demand NOT met (300 < 400) so revenue is capped at 300/400=75%; revenue=$51,940,000x75%=$38,955,000; profit=$38,955,000-$23,600,000=$15,355,000. Moosonee options both constrained and < Sudbury+Embraer. Saguenay both options satisfy demand but profit < $28M.
math.answer: Sudbury with Embraer E190 is the optimal choice. The Embraer is the only aircraft that can satisfy full demand at Sudbury (420 seats/day vs. 400 needed) within its 17 operating hours. Annual profit = ~$28.1M. The Bombardier cannot satisfy Sudbury demand, and Moosonee revenue is materially reduced by aircraft constraints regardless of aircraft chosen.

brainstorming.prompt: What types of costs would be relevant when choosing which aircraft to operate on a new route?

categories.name: Fuel Costs
ideas: Fuel burn per mile varies by aircraft type and size
Fuel efficiency at different load factors

categories.name: Maintenance Costs
ideas: Availability of maintenance staff at remote airports

categories.name: Crew Costs
ideas: Crew training and certification for specific aircraft type
Positioning costs to get crew to remote airports

categories.name: Capacity and Revenue Implications
ideas: Number of seats determines max revenue per flight

categories.name: Operational Constraints
ideas: Speed affects number of round trips possible per day
Regulatory restrictions on noise and night flying

recommendation: Maple Leaf Airlines should expand service to Sudbury Airport using the Embraer E190 aircraft, yielding estimated annual profit of approximately $28.1M
This is the only airport-aircraft combination that satisfies full passenger demand (420 seats/day capacity vs. 400 demand) within Sudbury's 17 operating hours (6:00-23:00)
Revenues exceed costs by well over 10%, satisfying the COO's threshold
risks: Sensitivity to % of business travelers: if fewer than 30% of Sudbury passengers are business travelers, revenue and profit will be lower than projected
Competitor response: incumbent carriers may lower prices or add capacity to defend the Sudbury market
Aircraft availability and maintenance downtime could reduce actual trips and revenue
Assumption that Maple Leaf can capture exactly 10% of market may not hold given competitive dynamics
Operating hours restrictions could change, affecting route economics
next_steps: Advise the client on customer acquisition strategy to reach rural fliers who need access to Sudbury
Refine ticket pricing model to maximize market capture while remaining competitive
Lobby Moosonee municipal authorities to extend airport operating hours (currently 7:00-20:00), which would make Moosonee the most profitable route
Explore whether a faster or higher-capacity aircraft could unlock full demand at Moosonee
Conduct NPV analysis of the lifetime value of the Sudbury expansion
Develop implementation plan including staffing, ground operations, and marketing launch
